                          detector = "multi",
                          covnames = 'sex')

                      buffer = 100,
                      type = "trapbuffer",
                      poly = land )

m.array(ebbCH)

fitspNull <- openCR.fit( ebbCH, type = 'JSSAsecrlCL', model = list( lambda0 ~ t, phi ~ t ),

Thanks,

Rebecca

messages.body_plain:

I've discretized my polygon data to the proximity detector type. Is there a way to get the new xy coordinates for the discretized capture history?

Thank you

messages.subject: Re: Trap coordinates from discretize()
messages.body_plain:
I think traps(CH1)[trap(CH1),] should do it. For example, extending the example for discretize:

library(secr)
pol <- make.poly()
CH <- sim.capthist(pol, popn = list(D = 30), detectpar = list(g0 = 0.3))
CH1 <- discretize(CH, spacing = 10, output = 'count')
cbind(animalID(CH1), occasion(CH1), traps(CH1)[trap(CH1),])

See also the plot at the end of Examples.

Murray

messages.body_plain:
The default detector type in read.traps() is 'multi' which refers to a multi-catch trap i.e. one that can catch multiple animals at once. With 'multi' detectors there is never more than one detection per animal per occasion - that's in the nature of traps.

Use read.traps(.. detector = 'proximity') to allow the possibility of multiple detections on one occasion.

Check with table(apply(tch.F, 1:2, sum))

I also suggest you play with secrdesignapp, or at least use it as a cross-check -

library(shiny)
runGitHub("secrdesignapp", "MurrayEfford")

"secr.fit scales the x- and y-coordinates of mask points to mean = 0, SD = 1 before using the coordinates
in a model. Remember this when you come to use the coefficients of a density model. Functions such as
predictDsurface take care of scaling automatically. predict.secr uses the scaled values (‘newdata’ x = 0,
y = 0), which provides the predicted density at the mask centroid. The mean and SD used in scaling are
those saved as the ‘meanSD’ attribute of a mask (dataframe with columns ‘x’ and ‘y’ and rows ‘mean’ and

Murray

messages.body_plain:
Hi Stefano
It should be possible to solve your mask problem. In my experience -
1. When a non-spatial model is fitted to data from spatial sampling, in general the estimates of phi will be slightly negatively biased (1-4%, which may or may not be acceptable depending on your application), and the nonspatial estimates of lambda will be essentially unbiased.
2. Things get worse if the spatial extent of sampling changes over time (exposing different sets of animals); then lambda-hat from the non-spatial model may be very biased (see e.g. Hines & Nichols 2002 J Applied Statistics) but the spatial estimates are OK.

I don't know if that applies in your case.

Murray

##Define function for non-euclidian distance
##from http://www.ecography.org/sites/ecography.org/files/appendix/ecog-01511.pdf
## Option 1: integrating along least-cost path
userdist1 <- function (xy1, xy2, mask) {
  if (missing(xy1)) return(c("D", "noneuc"))
  D <- covariates(mask)$D
  k <- covariates(mask)$noneuc ## noneuc = k
  sigma <- k / sqrt(D)
  if (!require(gdistance))
    stop ('install package gdistance to use this function')
  ## make raster from mask, assigning 1/sigma to all habitat cells
  Draster <- raster(mask, values = 1/sigma)
  ## Assume animals can traverse gaps: bridge gaps using mean
  Draster[is.na <http://is.na>(Draster[])] <- mean(Draster[], na.rm = TRUE)
  ## form gdistance ‘TransitionLayer’ to define cell-cell connections
  trfn <- function(x) 1 / mean(x)
  tr <- transition(Draster, transitionFunction = trfn, directions = 16)
  tr <- geoCorrection(tr, type = "c", multpl = FALSE)
  ## costDistance finds length of least-cost path
  distmat <- costDistance(tr, as.matrix(xy1), as.matrix(xy2))
  distmat[!is.finite(distmat)] <- 1e10 ## avoid infinite values
  distmat
}

plot(covariates(DS)$D.0, covariates(DS)$sigma)

userdist2 <- function (xy1, xy2, mask) {
  ## use addCovariates here to associate D with each point

  xy2 <- addCovariates(xy2, mask)
  D1 <- covariates(xy1)$D^0.5
  D2 <- covariates(xy2)$D^0.5

  euc <- edist(xy1, xy2)
  sig <- outer (D1, D2, FUN=function(d1,d2) k * (1/d1 + 1/d2)/2)
  euc / sig
}

You have a point (known variation in effort should be allowed for in non-spatial open CR) but that doesn't happen because my only mechanism for tracking effort is detector-specific, and detectors do not appear in the non-spatial model. My defence might be that the effect of varying effort is usually minor, but I suppose it matters if you care about the detection parameters themselves (just p, I suppose).
